That question is still being written — as recently as the last few decades, on the stone obelisk near where she was found, by a hand that was never caught either.

atalanta.reels:
January 1880, the Royal Naval Dockyard in Bermuda. The training ship HMS Atalanta sailed for England with about 280 aboard, most of them young trainees. She never arrived. None of them was ever seen again. Wreckage was reported near the Azores, but none of it was ever proven to be hers. A former crewman said she rolled dangerously; no trace of her was ever found. Theories include a storm and an unstable ship. No wreck has ever been identified.

Still unsolved.

stendec.reels:
August 2, 1947, over the Andes. The airliner Star Dust, flying from Buenos Aires to Santiago, sent its last message in Morse code: an arrival time four minutes away, then one word, STENDEC. The radio operator in Santiago asked again, and the same word came back twice more. The plane never arrived; its wreckage was found on Mount Tupungato in 1998. The crash itself is broadly understood: a descent in thick cloud while still over the mountains. No one aboard survived. The word has never been explained. Theories include a scrambled "descent" or a misheard Morse sign-off, but none has been confirmed.

Still unsolved.

#mystery #stendec #unsolved #aviation #history #andes #reels #stillunsolved

indusscript.reels:
More than 4,000 years ago, in the Indus Valley of present-day Pakistan and northwest India, people carved small stone seals, most with an animal and a short row of signs. More than 4,000 inscribed objects have been found. The average text is just five signs long, drawn from roughly 400 different signs. No bilingual text, no Rosetta Stone, has ever been found. Some scholars have argued the signs may not be writing at all. More than 100 decipherments have been proposed, and in 2025 the Tamil Nadu government offered a $1 million prize. No proposed reading has been accepted.

Still unsolved.

velaclues.reels:
September 1979. An American satellite recorded a double flash over the southern Indian Ocean. Hours later, the Arecibo radio telescope in Puerto Rico picked up a ripple in the upper atmosphere, moving in an unusual direction. Underwater sound recordings were later linked by a Navy laboratory study to a blast at sea. In October and November, iodine-131, a product of nuclear fission, turned up in the thyroids of sheep in southeastern Australia. In 1980, a panel convened for the White House judged the flash probably not a nuclear explosion. Many government scientists disagreed. No government has ever confirmed what it was.

Still unsolved.

#mystery #velaincident #coldwar #history #unsolved #nuclear #reels #stillunsolved

flannanlog.reels:
December 1900, the Flannan Isles lighthouse in Scotland's Outer Hebrides. The keepers' last log entries are often quoted: a great storm, a keeper weeping, and a final line, "God is over all." None of those words are in the official record. They were printed in a 1965 book, credited to a 1929 magazine story that the historian Mike Dash concluded was fiction. The official report says the log ended on 13 December, and a chalk slate carries the routine to the morning of the 15th: the lamp cleaned, the oil filled. The entries were invented. The disappearance was not. The three keepers were never found.

Still unsolved.

#flannanisles #lighthouse #scotland #hebrides #mystery #history #unsolved #stillunsolved

rongowood.reels:
2024. Scientists radiocarbon-dated four rongorongo tablets from Rapa Nui (Easter Island), kept in Rome. The wood of one, a notched tablet called Échancrée, came from a tree felled around 1500, more than two centuries before Europeans arrived in 1722. If the writing is that old, the islanders may have invented it on their own, as only a handful of places in history ever have. But dating the wood is not dating the carving, and the study's authors say so. That wood never grew on the island; it may have drifted ashore or come off a European ship. Some linguists question whether the script is full writing at all. Fewer than 30 inscribed objects survive, and the script has never been deciphered.

Still unsolved.

#rongorongo #rapanui #easterisland #archaeology #ancienthistory #mystery #unsolved #stillunsolved

celestedoyle.reels:
December 1872, the Atlantic between the Azores and Portugal. The brigantine Mary Celeste was found drifting with no one aboard. The "Marie Celeste" most people know comes from a young Arthur Conan Doyle, whose story ran unsigned in the Cornhill Magazine in 1884, three years before Sherlock Holmes. Told as a survivor's statement, it had the ship's boats still aboard, and even the American consul at Gibraltar asked whether it was true. In fact her only boat was gone, her cargo of alcohol was nearly untouched, and she carried food and water for six months. The story was invented. The empty ship was real. The ten people aboard were never found.

Still unsolved.

#maryceleste #conandoyle #ghostship #maritime #history #mystery #unsolved #stillunsolved

doraenigma.reels:
June 1899, London. Two years after Dora Penny received Edward Elgar's unreadable cipher, she became a piece of his music: Variation X, "Dorabella", in his Enigma Variations. In the programme for the first performance, Elgar said that another, larger theme goes through the whole set, but is not played. He told Dora he thought she, of all people, would guess it. She never did. Elgar died in 1934 without naming it. Dozens of answers have been proposed, and none has ever been generally accepted.

Still unsolved.

#mystery #elgar #enigmavariations #dorabella #classicalmusic #unsolved #history #stillunsolved

kobenhavn.reels:
December 1928, Buenos Aires. The Danish training ship København, a five-masted barque and then the largest sailing ship in the world, set out for Australia. 60 people were aboard, 45 of them cadets. Eight days out, she radioed a passing steamer that all was well. When it called her again, she did not answer. A search across the South Atlantic lasted months and found nothing. Reported sightings were never confirmed, and no one aboard was ever seen again.

Still unsolved.

#mystery #kobenhavn #unsolved #shipwreck #maritime #history #denmark #stillunsolved

waratahsearch.reels:
July 1909, off the coast of South Africa. The liner Waratah left Durban for Cape Town with 211 people aboard, and none was ever seen again. In 1999, searchers announced they had found her: explorer Emlyn Brown's sonar had located a wreck whose outline seemed to match. Two years later, a dive showed it was another ship, the Nailsea Meadow, a wartime freighter lost in 1943. In 2004, after more than twenty years, Brown said he had exhausted his options and no longer knew where to look. The Waratah has never been found.

Still unsolved.

#sswaratah #shipwreck #maritime #history #southafrica #mystery #unsolved #stillunsolved

voynichvellum.reels:
In 2009, a radiocarbon lab at the University of Arizona in Tucson tested four slivers of vellum from the Voynich manuscript, a book that has never been deciphered. One theory held that Wilfrid Voynich, the book dealer who bought it in 1912, had faked it himself. The four samples came from four different pages, and all four dated the skin to the early 1400s, roughly 1404 to 1438. That dates the skin, not the writing, and the ink itself was not dated. But nothing in the inks or paints was out of place for that time. A modern fake now looks unlikely. Yet no one has proved what a single word of it says.

Still unsolved.

startiger.reels:
January 30, 1948, over the Atlantic. The British airliner Star Tiger was flying through the night from the Azores to Bermuda, with 31 people aboard. Just after 3 a.m., she asked Bermuda for a radio bearing. Nothing more was heard. The search found no wreckage, and no one aboard was ever seen again. The official inquiry wrote that no more baffling problem had ever been presented for investigation. Theories include fuel running out, and sabotage. The wreck has never been found.

Still unsolved.

griffon.reels:
September 18, 1679, Lake Michigan. Le Griffon, the first full-sized sailing ship on the upper Great Lakes, sailed from Washington Island for Niagara. Her cargo was furs. Six men were aboard: her pilot and five crew. She never arrived, and no one aboard was ever seen again. A friar from the expedition wrote of a violent storm; La Salle believed his own crew had sunk her and taken the furs. Wrecks in Lake Michigan and Lake Huron have been claimed as hers. None has ever been confirmed.

Still unsolved.

#mystery #legriffon #greatlakes #shipwreck #lakemichigan #unsolved #history #stillunsolved

upsweep.reels:
August 1991, the Pacific Ocean. When NOAA began recording the Navy's undersea hydrophones, one sound was already there. A long train of rising tones, each several seconds long, loud enough to be recorded across the Pacific. It became known as Upsweep, and in the recordings it seems seasonal, peaking in spring and autumn. Its source lies roughly in the remote South Pacific, between New Zealand and South America. Whales were an early guess, but the tone barely varies. It lies near what may be undersea volcanic activity, and it has grown fainter since 1991. NOAA still calls its origin unresolved.

Still unsolved.

#mystery #upsweep #ocean #unexplainedsounds #noaa #unsolved #science #stillunsolved

ninthlegion.reels:
Around AD 108, York, Roman Britain. Rome's Ninth Legion was based at the fortress there. A stone carved for a gate of the fortress is its last securely dated record in Britain. By the 120s, another legion was at York. Tiles stamped with the Ninth's name turned up at Nijmegen, in the Netherlands, but when they were made is disputed. Later lists of Rome's legions do not include it. Lost in Britain, moved to the Rhine, or sent east: all remain theories.

Still unsolved.

#mystery #ninthlegion #romanbritain #ancientrome #history #unsolved #archaeology #stillunsolved

deeringbottle.reels:
April 1921, Buxton, near Cape Hatteras, North Carolina. A local fisherman turned in a note he said he had found in a bottle. Ten weeks earlier, the schooner Carroll A. Deering had been found aground on Diamond Shoals, sails set, her crew gone. The note claimed the Deering had been captured by another boat. Five federal departments investigated, and handwriting experts concluded the note was forged. The fisherman later admitted forging it, reportedly hoping for work at the lighthouse. The real crew was never found.

Still unsolved.

#carrolladeering #ghostship #messageinabottle #capehatteras #outerbanks #maritimehistory #unsolved #stillunsolved

roanokestone.reels:
2012, the British Museum, London. Researchers lit a map from beneath. It was drawn more than four centuries ago by John White, governor of the Roanoke colony. Under a small paper patch was a hidden fort symbol in bright red and blue, where the Roanoke and Chowan rivers meet. In 1590, White had found his colony deserted, with CROATOAN carved on a post. He wrote that the settlers had planned to move fifty miles inland. Digs near that spot have found a few English pottery sherds. Why the symbol was covered is unknown, and where the colonists went has never been proved.

Still unsolved.

#lostcolony #roanoke #history #mystery #archaeology #unsolved #reels #stillunsolved

velasat.reels:
September 22, 1979, the southern Indian Ocean. One American satellite, Vela 6911, recorded a double flash of light. Vela satellites had recorded 41 double flashes before, and every one had been a nuclear test. But this satellite was ten years old, past its design life, and its radio-pulse sensor had already failed. Its two light sensors both caught the flash, yet their readings disagreed on the second pulse. In 1980, a panel for the White House suggested a tiny meteoroid had struck the satellite, its debris catching the sun. Later analysis judged a meteoroid much less likely, and other evidence pointed to a test. The United States has never confirmed what its satellite saw.

Still unsolved.

#mystery #velaincident #coldwar #satellite #history #unsolved #space #stillunsolved

starariel.reels:
January 17, 1949, Bermuda. Less than a year after the Star Tiger vanished, British South American Airways sent the same kind of airliner, an Avro Tudor IV named Star Ariel, to Kingston, Jamaica. This time the weather was fine, and the captain reported good visibility. About an hour out, he sent a routine message: he was changing radio frequency. Nothing more was heard. Warships and aircraft searched for days and found no wreckage at all. The inquiry could not find a cause, and the wreck has never been found.

Still unsolved.

devilsprints.reels:
February 1855, south Devon, England. After a night of heavy snow, people woke to find lines of small hoof-shaped prints, about four inches long, mostly in single file. They were reported in more than 30 places, on both sides of the Exe estuary, and reports said they crossed rooftops and high walls. Some said the Devil had walked, and it was spoken of from the pulpit. One letter at the time claimed a trail ran over a hundred miles in a single night; the farthest anyone is known to have followed one was about five miles. Donkeys, wood mice, a runaway balloon and a hoax have all been suggested. None has ever explained every mark.

Still unsolved.

bathurst.reels:
November 25, 1809, Perleberg, Prussia. Benjamin Bathurst, a British envoy, was travelling home from Vienna under a false name. Around nine that night, he stepped out of the White Swan inn while his carriage was readied, and was never seen again. Three weeks later, two women gathering firewood found his trousers in a wood outside the town, with a letter to his wife in a pocket. Some believed he was robbed; others blamed French agents. Napoleon said he knew nothing of it. In 1852 a skeleton was found beneath a house in the town, but it was never identified as his.

Still unsolved.

celestehold.reels:
December 4, 1872, the Atlantic near the Azores. The men who boarded the empty brigantine Mary Celeste found a sounding rod on her deck, a tool for measuring water in the hold. Nearby, one of her two pumps had been partly taken apart. Two hatches stood open, and below was about three and a half feet of water, not enough to sink her. One theory is that a false reading convinced the captain she was sinking, and everyone left in her only boat. Her cargo of alcohol was nearly untouched, she had food and water for six months, and she was sailed on to Gibraltar. Not one of the ten people who had sailed on her was ever seen again.

Still unsolved.
